section_1.title: Introduction: The Intuitive Hook
section_1.content: Present the visual problem: Can you always fit a square inside a closed loop (like a squiggle on a piece of paper)? Introduce the concept of a 'Jordan Curve'.
section_1.example: An artist drawing a continuous, non-intersecting line (a snake) on a canvas; can we always place four corners of a square on that line?

section_2.title: Prerequisite: The Configuration Space
section_2.content: Explain that we aren't just looking at the loop, but at a 2D space of 'candidate squares' defined by their center and size, mapping these points to the loop boundary.
section_2.example: Visualizing a 3D coordinate system where the x and y axes represent the center of the square, and the z-axis represents its side length.

section_3.title: The Mathematical Mechanism: Symmetry & Topology
section_3.content: Introduce the Borsuk-Ulam Theorem: A continuous map from a sphere to a plane must map antipodal points to the same value. Use this to prove that a square must exist.
section_3.example: Using a globe projection: If you have two points on exactly opposite sides of the earth, their 'temperature' or 'pressure' values will match.

section_4.title: Visualizing the Inscription
section_4.content: Demonstrate the transition from a candidate set to the final intersection. Show how shrinking/rotating the square until all four vertices touch the curve satisfies the topology condition.
section_4.example: Animation of a robot arm 'sliding' a square template along a curvy path until all four corners click into place simultaneously.

section_5.title: Conclusion & Generalizations
section_5.content: Briefly touch upon the 'Inscribed Rectangle' problem (which is proven for any Jordan curve) and mention that the 'Square' version is still an active research area for non-smooth curves.
section_5.example: Comparison: A rectangle is easy to 'stretch' into place, whereas a square is 'rigid,' explaining why the math gets harder.
